content: Pertussis, commonly referred to as whooping cough, is a highly contagious respiratory disease caused by the bacterium Bordetella pertussis. This condition is characterized by episodes of uncontrollable and violent coughing, which can make it difficult for individuals to breathe. While pertussis can affect individuals of all ages, it poses a particularly severe risk to infants under one year of age, as it can lead to life-threatening complications or even death. The disease spreads from person to person through respiratory droplets, such as those produced when an infected individual coughs, sneezes, or shares the same breathing space with others. In its early stages, pertussis symptoms are often mild and resemble those of a common cold. These symptoms may include a runny nose, low-grade fever, and a mild cough. However, as the disease progresses, more severe symptoms can develop. These include episodes of rapid, consecutive coughing fits followed by a high-pitched whoop sound during inhalation, vomiting after coughing, and extreme fatigue. These coughing fits can persist for up to 10 weeks or longer. In infants, the characteristic cough may be absent or minimal, but they may experience pauses in breathing, known as apnea. Pertussis is a global disease, but it is more prevalent in developing countries where vaccination rates are low. Each year, approximately one million cases of pertussis occur worldwide, resulting in an estimated 160,700 deaths among children under the age of five. To prevent pertussis, staying up to date with vaccinations is the most effective strategy. Pertussis vaccines are typically administered as combination vaccines that also protect against diphtheria and tetanus. For infants and children: Babies require three doses of the DTaP vaccine to build strong immunity against diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis. Young children then need two booster doses to maintain this protection during early childhood. For preteens and teens: Preteens should receive a single dose of the Tdap vaccine between the ages of 11 and 12 to boost their immunity. Teens who missed this dose during preadolescence should receive it at their next healthcare visit. For pregnant women: Pregnant women are advised to receive the Tdap vaccine during the early part of the third trimester of every pregnancy. This helps protect their newborns from pertussis during the first few months of life, when they are most vulnerable. For adults: Adults who have never received a Tdap vaccine should get one at any time, regardless of when they last received a tetanus (Td) vaccine. After this initial dose, adults should receive either a Td or Tdap booster every 10 years. By adhering to these vaccination guidelines, individuals can significantly reduce the risk of contracting and spreading pertussis.
